title: Plate Tectonics: How Geology Learned That the Continents Move
summary: From Wegener's ridiculed idea of drifting continents to the magnetic stripes on the seafloor that settled the argument: how plate tectonics became the theory that explains earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.
body:
Look at a world map and something odd jumps out almost at once. The bulge of Brazil looks as if it would slot neatly into the hollow of West Africa, like two pieces of a jigsaw puzzle that someone pulled apart and then forgot about. Schoolchildren notice it. So did mapmakers almost as soon as the coastlines of the Atlantic were charted well enough to compare. For centuries, though, the observation was treated as a curiosity, a coincidence of geography with no deeper meaning. Continents, after all, were the very picture of permanence. Mountains might rise and wear down over unimaginable spans of time, seas might flood and retreat, but the idea that whole continents could wander across the face of the planet seemed absurd.

Today almost every geologist on Earth accepts that the continents do move, that the ocean floors are continuously being created and destroyed, and that the outer shell of the planet is broken into a few large slabs that grind against one another at about the speed your fingernails grow. This framework, called **plate tectonics**, is to geology what evolution is to biology: the idea that makes sense of everything else. It explains why earthquakes cluster where they do, why volcanoes form chains and rings, why the Himalayas are still rising, why the Atlantic is getting wider and the Pacific is getting narrower, and why fossils of the same land reptile turn up on continents now separated by thousands of kilometres of ocean.

What makes the story especially worth telling is how the idea arrived. It was proposed in a fairly complete form early in the twentieth century, rejected by most experts for about four decades, and then accepted with astonishing speed in the 1960s once new kinds of evidence came in from the bottom of the sea. It is one of the clearest cases in modern science of a revolution in thinking, and it carries lessons about evidence, mechanism, stubbornness and humility that reach well beyond rocks.

## The world before drift

To understand why continental drift seemed so outlandish, it helps to know what geologists believed before it. In the nineteenth century the dominant explanation for mountains and ocean basins was that the Earth was slowly cooling and shrinking. A cooling body contracts, the reasoning went, and as the interior shrank, the solid crust would wrinkle like the skin of a drying apple. Mountain ranges were the wrinkles. Ocean basins were places where great blocks of crust had sunk.

This contraction theory had a certain elegance, and it fitted the idea, common at the time, that the Earth had begun as a molten ball and had been losing heat ever since. But it also had problems. If the whole planet were shrinking, mountains should be spread fairly evenly across its surface, yet they are concentrated in long, narrow belts. And by the early twentieth century physicists had discovered radioactivity, which meant the Earth's interior had its own continuing source of heat. A planet warmed from within by decaying uranium, thorium and potassium would not necessarily be cooling and shrinking in the simple way the theory needed.

There was also the puzzle of fossils. Paleontologists had found that certain plants and animals appeared on continents that are now far apart. To explain this, many geologists proposed "land bridges": narrow strips of land that had once connected, say, South America and Africa, letting animals walk across, and that had later sunk beneath the ocean. The bridges were invented to solve a problem, and there was no independent evidence for them. Nobody could say how a continent-sized strip of land could simply sink and vanish.

Into this situation stepped a man who was not, by training, a geologist at all.

## Alfred Wegener and the idea of continental drift

Alfred Wegener (1880–1930) was a German scientist whose main fields were meteorology and polar research. He studied astronomy, became an expert on the physics of the atmosphere, flew weather balloons, and took part in expeditions to Greenland. He was, in other words, an outsider to the geology establishment, and that fact would matter a great deal in how his idea was received.

Wegener was struck by the matching coastlines of the Atlantic, but he did not stop at shapes. He began collecting evidence from many fields. In January 1912 he presented his idea in a lecture in Frankfurt, and he developed it at book length in *Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane* (*The Origin of Continents and Oceans*), first published in 1915 and revised several times in the following years. His argument was that the continents had once been joined in a single supercontinent, which he later called **Pangaea** (Greek for "all lands"), and that this landmass had broken apart, with the pieces slowly drifting to their present positions.

What made Wegener's case powerful was the variety of evidence he assembled:

- **The fit of the continents.** The match between South America and Africa is even better if you use the edge of the continental shelf, a few hundred metres below sea level, rather than the present coastline, which shifts with sea level.
- **Matching rocks and mountain belts.** Rock formations and the remains of ancient mountain ranges seemed to line up across the Atlantic. Old mountains in eastern North America, for instance, have counterparts in Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia.
- **Fossils.** The small freshwater reptile *Mesosaurus* is found in southern Africa and in South America, but nowhere else. It could hardly have swum across an ocean. The fossil seed fern *Glossopteris* turns up across the southern continents, including Antarctica and India.
- **Ancient climates.** Wegener, the climate scientist, paid special attention to rocks that record past climates. Coal deposits, which form from lush vegetation, are found in places that are now cold. Scratches and debris left by glaciers are found in places that are now tropical or close to it, such as parts of India, Africa and South America. If the continents had stayed put, the climate patterns of the past made little sense. If they had moved, the evidence fell into place: these lands had once been grouped together near the South Pole.

Wegener was a careful thinker, and he understood that his evidence was circumstantial. Each line alone could be explained away. Together, he argued, they formed a pattern that the fixed-continent view could not easily account for. He compared it to tearing a newspaper in two: if the lines of print match across the torn edges, you can be fairly sure the pieces belong together.

## Why the experts said no

Wegener's idea attracted interest, and a few geologists were enthusiastic, notably Alexander du Toit in South Africa, who added a great deal of geological detail on the matching rocks of the southern continents. But most of the geological community, particularly in Britain and North America, rejected it, sometimes with real hostility. At an often-cited meeting of the American Association of Petroleum Geologists in New York in 1926, the idea was given a hearing and largely dismissed.

It is easy, with hindsight, to treat the critics as fools. They were not. Their central objection was a serious one: Wegener had no convincing **mechanism**. If continents move, what pushes them? Wegener suggested forces related to the Earth's rotation and to the tidal pull of the Moon and Sun. Physicists, including the influential British geophysicist Harold Jeffreys, showed that these forces were far too weak to shove continents around. Wegener also pictured the continents ploughing through the ocean floor like ships through ice, and critics pointed out that the rocks of the ocean floor are too strong for that. A continent pushing through solid rock would crumple before it moved.

There were other reasons too. Some of Wegener's estimates of drift speed were far too high; he suggested that Greenland might be moving away from Europe at many metres per year, a figure that later measurements did not support. Geologists also had professional and cultural reasons to be wary. Wegener was an outsider. His theory required tearing up a great deal of established work. And the scientific culture of the time, especially in the United States, valued careful local fieldwork and distrusted sweeping global theories built on assembled evidence from many places.

The lesson here is a subtle one. The critics were right that Wegener's proposed mechanism did not work. They were wrong to conclude that the phenomenon he described therefore did not exist. Science often accepts that something happens before it understands why. But in the case of drift, the lack of a mechanism was treated as fatal.

Wegener did not live to see his idea vindicated. In November 1930, during an expedition on the Greenland ice sheet, he died while returning from a camp in the interior, apparently of heart failure brought on by exhaustion and cold. His body was found the following spring. He was fifty.

## Arthur Holmes and a hint of the answer

One scientist did offer a mechanism that, in outline, turned out to be close to right. The British geologist Arthur Holmes, a pioneer of using radioactivity to date rocks, proposed around 1930 that heat from radioactive decay inside the Earth could drive slow **convection currents** in the mantle, the thick layer of hot rock beneath the crust. Hot rock rises, spreads sideways, cools and sinks, much as water circulates in a pot on a stove. Holmes suggested that such currents could drag continents apart, with new ocean floor forming where currents rose and old crust being pulled down where they sank.

The mantle is solid rock, so the idea that it flows may seem strange. But over millions of years, rock under enormous heat and pressure can deform slowly, a bit like the way glacier ice, which is solid, nonetheless flows downhill. Holmes's proposal was largely speculative, though, and he presented it cautiously. Without direct evidence from the ocean floor, it did not change many minds.

That evidence would come from an unexpected place: the needs of navies and the technologies of war.

## The ocean floor speaks

Before the Second World War, the deep ocean floor was almost completely unknown. Measuring depth meant lowering a weighted line, a slow process that gave one reading at a time. During and after the war, the development of **echo sounding**, which bounces sound pulses off the seabed and times their return, allowed ships to record continuous profiles of the ocean floor as they sailed. Navies wanted to know the terrain under the sea for submarine warfare, and they funded a great deal of research.

### Marie Tharp maps a crack in the world

At the Lamont Geological Observatory of Columbia University in New York, a geologist and cartographer named Marie Tharp began working in the late 1940s and early 1950s with Bruce Heezen, who collected echo-sounding data from research cruises. Women were not allowed on the research ships at the time, so Tharp worked from the data, plotting thousands of depth soundings by hand to build profiles of the Atlantic floor.

Around 1952, she noticed something remarkable. Along the crest of the great underwater mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, there appeared to be a deep V-shaped notch: a **rift valley**, a place where the crust seemed to be pulling apart. Heezen was initially dismissive, reportedly calling it "girl talk," because a rift implied that the ocean floor was splitting, which sounded too much like continental drift. But the evidence held up, especially when it was found that earthquakes in the Atlantic were concentrated along the same line.

Tharp and Heezen went on to map the ridge system and found that it was not just an Atlantic feature. Mid-ocean ridges run through all the world's oceans, winding around the planet like the seam on a baseball, forming a connected system tens of thousands of kilometres long. It is the largest mountain range on Earth, and almost all of it is underwater. Their maps, culminating in the *World Ocean Floor* panorama painted with the Austrian artist Heinrich Berann and published in 1977, gave the public its first vivid picture of the hidden landscape of the deep sea. Tharp's contribution was underappreciated for decades and has only in recent years received the recognition it deserves.

### Harry Hess and seafloor spreading

Harry Hess, a Princeton geologist who had commanded a US Navy transport ship during the war and kept its echo sounder running as he crossed the Pacific, had his own observations of the seafloor. Drawing together the new findings, he proposed in a paper circulated around 1960 and published in 1962 as "History of Ocean Basins" that the ocean floor is not permanent at all. New crust, he suggested, forms at the mid-ocean ridges where hot material wells up from the mantle. It then spreads outward on both sides like two conveyor belts moving away from each other. Far from the ridges, old ocean floor sinks back into the mantle at the deep ocean trenches.

Hess was cautious enough to call his paper "an essay in geopoetry," acknowledging that it went beyond the hard evidence available. Around the same time, the American geophysicist Robert Dietz proposed a very similar idea and gave it the name that stuck: **seafloor spreading**.

Seafloor spreading neatly solved several puzzles at once. It explained why the ocean floor is surprisingly thin and young compared with the continents, and why it carries relatively little sediment: it simply has not been around long enough to accumulate much. It also removed Wegener's biggest problem. Continents do not plough through the ocean floor. They ride along with it, carried passively as the conveyor belts move.

But geopoetry needed a test. That test came from magnetism.

## Magnetic stripes: the decisive evidence

The Earth behaves like a giant magnet, and its magnetic field has a curious habit: every so often, over intervals ranging from tens of thousands to millions of years, it **reverses**. Magnetic north becomes magnetic south and vice versa. By the early 1960s, scientists studying lava flows on land had established that such reversals had happened many times, and they were building a timeline of when.

When lava cools, tiny grains of iron-bearing minerals within it line up with the Earth's magnetic field at that moment, like miniature compass needles frozen in place. The rock thus preserves a record of the field's direction at the time it solidified.

Meanwhile, ships towing sensitive magnetometers across the ocean had discovered a bizarre pattern. Off the west coast of North America, the magnetic strength of the seafloor varied in long stripes running parallel to the ocean ridges: bands of slightly stronger magnetism alternating with bands of slightly weaker. Nobody knew what to make of it.

In 1963, Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews, working at the University of Cambridge, published a short paper in the journal *Nature* proposing an explanation. The Canadian geologist Lawrence Morley had reached the same idea independently but had his paper rejected by journals, so the hypothesis is now often called the **Vine–Matthews–Morley hypothesis**. The idea was this: if new crust forms at the ridge and spreads outward, and if the Earth's magnetic field flips from time to time, then each strip of new crust will record the field direction at the time it formed. The result should be a pattern of stripes of normal and reversed magnetism running parallel to the ridge, and the pattern on one side of the ridge should be a mirror image of the pattern on the other.

That is exactly what the measurements showed. Over the next few years, as more data were gathered, particularly across the Reykjanes Ridge south of Iceland and the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge, the symmetry became unmistakable. Better still, the widths of the stripes matched the timeline of reversals worked out independently from lavas on land. The ocean floor was a tape recorder, playing back the history of the Earth's magnetic field, and the tape had clearly been moving outward from the ridges.

For many geologists this was the moment the argument turned. Magnetic stripes were not circumstantial in the way Wegener's fossils were. They were a precise prediction of seafloor spreading that was then confirmed by measurement.

## From spreading to plates

Seafloor spreading explained how ocean floor was created, but a complete theory needed to explain the geometry of the whole planet's surface. Several pieces came together in a remarkably short period, roughly from 1965 to 1968.

The Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson recognised a new kind of fault, which he called the **transform fault**. Mid-ocean ridges are not continuous lines; they are broken into offset segments connected by faults running at right angles. Wilson showed that these faults behave differently from what one would expect if the ridge had simply been broken and shifted. They are boundaries where two pieces of crust slide past each other as each moves away from its own ridge segment. Wilson's paper of 1965 also introduced the idea of a set of rigid, interconnected plates whose boundaries are ridges, trenches and transform faults.

Then, in 1967 and 1968, Dan McKenzie and Robert Parker in Britain, W. Jason Morgan at Princeton, and Xavier Le Pichon at Lamont independently worked out the mathematics. On a sphere, the motion of any rigid piece of the surface relative to another can be described as a rotation about an axis through the Earth's centre, a principle that goes back to the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler. Using this, they showed that the motions of the large pieces of the Earth's surface could be described consistently, and that their predicted motions matched the directions of transform faults and the slip directions of earthquakes.

At around the same time, seismologists Bryan Isacks, Jack Oliver and Lynn Sykes at Lamont showed that earthquakes beneath ocean trenches occur along zones that slope down into the mantle, tracing the path of ocean floor being pushed back into the Earth. These sloping zones had been noticed earlier by Kiyoo Wadati in Japan and Hugo Benioff in the United States, and they are often called Wadati–Benioff zones.

By the end of the 1960s, the pieces fitted. The term "plate tectonics" was in use, and within a few years it had gone from a radical proposal to the foundation of textbooks. A few prominent geologists held out into the 1970s, but the change was swift by the standards of scientific revolutions.

One more confirmation came from drilling. The Deep Sea Drilling Project, which began in 1968 with the drilling ship *Glomar Challenger*, pulled up cores from the ocean floor and found that the sediments resting directly on the volcanic crust got progressively older with distance from the mid-ocean ridges, exactly as seafloor spreading predicted. No part of the ocean floor has been found to be much older than about 180 to 200 million years, while rocks on the continents can be billions of years old. The oceans are constantly being recycled; the continents, being lighter, mostly are not.

## How plate tectonics works

With the history in place, it is worth laying out the theory itself clearly.

### The layers that matter

The Earth's outer rocky shell is called the **lithosphere** (from the Greek for "stone sphere"). It includes the crust and the uppermost part of the mantle, and it behaves as a rigid, brittle layer. It is typically on the order of 100 kilometres thick, thinner under young ocean floor and thicker under old continents.

Beneath it lies the **asthenosphere** ("weak sphere"), a layer of the mantle that is hot enough to be slightly soft and able to flow slowly over geological time. The asthenosphere is not a sea of liquid magma, as is sometimes imagined. It is overwhelmingly solid rock, but rock that can deform plastically.

The lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the asthenosphere. There are about seven or eight major plates (the Pacific, North American, Eurasian, African, Antarctic, Indo-Australian, which some scientists divide into separate Indian and Australian plates, and South American) along with a number of smaller ones, such as the Nazca, Philippine Sea, Arabian, Caribbean, Cocos and Juan de Fuca plates. Plates are not the same as continents. Most plates carry both continental and oceanic crust; the North American plate, for example, includes the western half of the Atlantic floor.

There is an important difference between the two kinds of crust. **Oceanic crust** is made mostly of basalt, a dark, dense volcanic rock, and is relatively thin, usually around 6 to 7 kilometres. **Continental crust** is more varied, with a lot of lighter, granite-like rock, and is much thicker, typically 30 to 50 kilometres and more beneath large mountain ranges. Because continental crust is lighter, it tends to float high and resist being pulled down into the mantle. That is why continents survive for billions of years while ocean floors are recycled.

### Three kinds of boundaries

Almost all the action happens at plate boundaries. There are three basic types.

1. **Divergent boundaries**, where plates move apart. In the oceans these are the mid-ocean ridges, where magma rises to fill the gap and creates new oceanic crust. Iceland is a rare place where a mid-ocean ridge rises above sea level, which is one reason it has so many volcanoes and why visitors can stand in a valley between the North American and Eurasian plates. On land, divergence produces rift valleys. The East African Rift is the best-known example of a continent beginning to split; if it continues, part of eastern Africa may eventually separate and a new ocean may form.

2. **Convergent boundaries**, where plates move toward each other. What happens depends on what kind of crust is involved. When oceanic crust meets continental crust, the denser oceanic plate sinks beneath the continent in a process called **subduction**, forming a deep trench offshore and a line of volcanoes on land. The Andes of South America formed this way, as the Nazca plate dives beneath the South American plate. When two oceanic plates meet, one subducts under the other, producing a trench and an arc of volcanic islands; Japan, the Mariana Islands and the Aleutians are examples. The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific contains the deepest known point in the oceans, the Challenger Deep, roughly 11 kilometres below sea level. When two continents collide, neither sinks easily because both are buoyant, so the crust crumples and thickens into great mountain ranges. The Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau are the result of India colliding with Asia, a collision that began roughly 50 million years ago and is still under way.

3. **Transform boundaries**, where plates slide past each other horizontally. Crust is neither created nor destroyed. The San Andreas Fault in California, where the Pacific plate moves northwest relative to the North American plate, is the most famous example on land. Because the plates do not slide smoothly but stick and then suddenly slip, transform boundaries can produce large earthquakes.

### How fast, and what drives it

Plates move at speeds of a few centimetres per year. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads at around 2 to 5 centimetres per year, which is why the Atlantic Ocean widens by roughly the length of a fingernail's yearly growth. Some parts of the East Pacific Rise spread much faster, at over 10 centimetres per year. These speeds sound trivial, but over geological time they add up: at 5 centimetres per year, a plate moves 50 kilometres in a million years and 5,000 kilometres in a hundred million years. That is enough to open an ocean.

Today these motions can be measured directly. Satellite-based positioning systems such as GPS, along with older techniques that bounce signals off distant quasars or satellites, can track the positions of ground stations to millimetre precision. The measured motions agree well with the rates calculated from magnetic stripes over millions of years. Wegener's critics wanted a measurement; they now have one in every geophysics lab.

What actually drives the plates remains an area of active research, but the broad picture is clear. Mantle convection, as Holmes suggested, is part of it: the Earth is losing internal heat, and the slow churning of the mantle is how much of that heat gets out. But the plates are not simply passive rafts carried along by currents underneath. Many geophysicists think the most important force is **slab pull**: old oceanic crust is cold and dense, and where it sinks into the mantle at a subduction zone, its weight drags the rest of the plate along behind it. Plates attached to large subducting slabs, such as the Pacific plate, tend to move fastest. A second force, **ridge push**, comes from the fact that new crust at mid-ocean ridges sits high and tends to slide downhill away from the ridge. In a real sense, the plates are part of the convection system: their cooling and sinking is one of the main ways the mantle circulates.

## What plate tectonics explains

The power of the theory is in how much it ties together.

### Earthquakes

If you plot the world's earthquakes on a map, they form narrow belts that trace the plate boundaries almost exactly. The great majority occur where plates meet. The largest earthquakes of all, often called megathrust earthquakes, happen at subduction zones, where one plate sticks against the other for centuries, builds up strain, and then lurches forward. The 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake in the Indian Ocean (magnitude about 9.1) and the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake off Japan (about magnitude 9.0 to 9.1) were both of this kind, and both caused devastating tsunamis because the seafloor itself was suddenly lifted, displacing an enormous volume of water.

### Volcanoes

Most volcanoes also sit along plate boundaries. At subduction zones, water carried down with the sinking plate lowers the melting point of the overlying mantle, producing magma that rises to feed volcanoes. This is the origin of the so-called **Ring of Fire**, the horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquake zones that encircles much of the Pacific Ocean, from the Andes through Central America, the Cascades, Alaska, Kamchatka, Japan, the Philippines and Indonesia to New Zealand. At mid-ocean ridges, the eruptions are mostly quiet outpourings of basalt on the seafloor.

Some volcanoes, though, sit far from any plate boundary. The Hawaiian Islands lie in the middle of the Pacific plate. Tuzo Wilson proposed in 1963 that such islands form over **hotspots**, places where hot material rises from deep in the mantle. As the plate moves over a fixed or slowly moving hotspot, a chain of volcanoes forms, each one older than the next. The Hawaiian chain does just that: the Big Island, with its active volcanoes, is youngest, and the islands get progressively older and more eroded toward the northwest, continuing as a line of submerged seamounts. Yellowstone in the United States is often explained as a hotspot beneath a continent, though the details of how hotspots work are still debated.

### Mountains

Mountain ranges are the scars of plate collisions. The Andes are a subduction-zone range. The Himalayas, the Alps and the Zagros Mountains of Iran are the result of continents colliding. Even old, worn-down ranges such as the Appalachians in North America and the Caledonian mountains of Scotland and Norway record collisions hundreds of millions of years ago, during the assembly of Pangaea. The fact that marine fossils are found high in the Himalayas, in rocks that were once sediment on the floor of an ocean that lay between India and Asia, is a vivid reminder of how much the surface can be rearranged.

### Fossils and the history of life

The scattered fossils that puzzled nineteenth-century scientists, from *Mesosaurus* to *Glossopteris* to the stocky plant-eating reptile *Lystrosaurus*, found in Africa, India and Antarctica, now have a simple explanation. These species lived on connected land, which later broke apart. Plate tectonics also helps explain patterns in living species. Australia's unusual animals, including its many marsupials, reflect its long isolation after it separated from Antarctica. The joining of North and South America through the Isthmus of Panama, a few million years ago, allowed animals to cross between continents in what biologists call the Great American Biotic Interchange.

### Resources

The theory has practical value too. Many metal ores, such as copper deposits in the Andes, form in association with subduction-zone magmas. Oil and gas accumulate in sedimentary basins whose formation is tied to rifting and the movement of plates. Understanding plate history helps geologists know where to look.

## Supercontinents come and go

Pangaea was not unique. Geologists now think that continents have repeatedly gathered into supercontinents and then split apart, in a pattern sometimes called the **supercontinent cycle** or, in honour of its proposer, the Wilson cycle, describing the opening and closing of ocean basins.

Pangaea itself assembled roughly 335 million years ago and began to break apart about 200 million years ago, in the early Jurassic period, with the opening of the central Atlantic. Before Pangaea there was probably an earlier supercontinent, often called Rodinia, which assembled around a billion years ago and broke up several hundred million years later. Before that, many researchers propose another, often called Columbia or Nuna. The further back one goes, the harder it is to reconstruct the details, because so much old ocean floor has been destroyed and continents have been broken and welded together many times.

Looking forward, some geologists have tried to predict the next supercontinent. Since the Atlantic is widening and the Pacific is shrinking, one scenario has the Pacific eventually closing, bringing the Americas back toward Asia. Other models suggest different arrangements. These forecasts reach hundreds of millions of years into the future and are best thought of as informed speculation, but they rest on the same principles that explain the present.

## Open questions

Plate tectonics is settled science in its broad outline, but it is not finished science. Several questions remain lively.

- **When did it start?** The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Whether plate tectonics in its modern form has been operating for most of that time, or began only around 3 billion years ago or later, is debated. The young, hot Earth may have behaved differently, perhaps with a single rigid lid or with many small, fast-moving plates.
- **Why only Earth?** Among the rocky planets of our solar system, Earth is the only one known to have active plate tectonics today. Venus, almost the same size, appears to have a single shell, though it shows signs of volcanic and tectonic activity of other kinds. Mars may have had some early tectonic activity but has none like Earth's now. Water may be part of the reason: it weakens rocks and may help plates break and subduct.
- **Plumes and hotspots.** Whether hotspots are fed by narrow plumes rising from the base of the mantle, nearly 3,000 kilometres down, or by shallower processes is still argued over.
- **Plates and life.** Some scientists argue that plate tectonics helps make Earth habitable by recycling carbon between the atmosphere, oceans and interior over long timescales, which helps stabilise climate. If that is right, it may matter in the search for habitable planets elsewhere.

## What the story teaches

The rise of plate tectonics is often told as a tale of a lone genius proved right after his death, and there is truth in that. Wegener saw the pattern before others did and argued for it with skill and persistence. But the full story is more interesting than a simple morality tale.

First, Wegener was not right about everything. His proposed mechanisms were wrong and his speed estimates were too high. The theory that eventually triumphed was different from his in important ways: continents ride on moving plates that include ocean floor, rather than ploughing through it. Science advanced not because one person was right but because many people, often working on what seemed to be unrelated problems, gathered evidence that eventually converged.

Second, the critics had a point. A scientific claim that something happens but cannot explain how is genuinely weaker than one that comes with a mechanism. The mistake was in treating the lack of a mechanism as proof that the phenomenon was impossible. "We don't know how this could work" is a reason for caution and further research, not for dismissal.

Third, new tools change what can be known. The decisive evidence came from technologies developed for very different purposes: echo sounders, magnetometers built partly for detecting submarines, and networks of seismometers set up in part to monitor nuclear tests. The ocean floor had been carrying a record of the Earth's history all along. It took the right instruments to read it.

Finally, the story is a reminder that even the most solid-seeming things can be in motion. The ground beneath your feet is moving right now, by a few centimetres a year, carried on a slab of rock that was once part of a different continent, and will one day be somewhere else entirely. The map on the classroom wall is only a single frame in a very long film.

## A short timeline

- **1912**: Alfred Wegener presents the idea of continental drift in a lecture in Frankfurt.
- **1915**: *The Origin of Continents and Oceans* is first published.
- **Around 1930**: Arthur Holmes proposes mantle convection as a driving force.
- **1930**: Wegener dies on the Greenland ice sheet.
- **Around 1952**: Marie Tharp identifies a rift valley along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
- **1961–1962**: Robert Dietz and Harry Hess propose seafloor spreading.
- **1963**: Vine and Matthews (and, independently, Morley) explain magnetic stripes on the seafloor.
- **1965**: Tuzo Wilson describes transform faults and a network of plates.
- **1967–1968**: McKenzie and Parker, Morgan, and Le Pichon work out the geometry of plate motions on a sphere.
- **1968 onward**: Deep-sea drilling confirms that ocean floor gets older with distance from the ridges.
- **1977**: Tharp and Heezen's *World Ocean Floor* map is published.
